description: 1688, the Bill of Rights and how a Protestant monarchy reshaped British power at home and abroad.
content_html:
The Crisis of 1688

By 1688, England was on the brink of a constitutional crisis. James II had ruled since 1685, and his reign had provoked widespread anxiety among Protestant elites. He promoted Catholics to senior positions in the army and government, issued the Declaration of Indulgence (1687) to suspend laws against Catholics and Dissenters, and had a son born in June 1688 — raising the prospect of a Catholic succession. Seven leading English nobles wrote to William of Orange, Mary’s husband, inviting him to intervene.

Key Fact

William of Orange landed at Brixham, Devon, on 5 November 1688 with an army of around 15,000 men. James II’s support collapsed almost immediately — key officers defected, including John Churchill (later Duke of Marlborough). James fled to France in December 1688.

Historians debate whether the term “Glorious Revolution” is accurate. Whig historians celebrated it as a bloodless assertion of parliamentary liberty. Jacobite and Catholic commentators, however, saw it as a Dutch invasion that displaced a legitimate Catholic king and imposed a Protestant constitutional settlement by force. Irish Catholics paid a particularly heavy price (see Lesson 2). The label “glorious” is a contested historiographic choice, not a neutral description.

William III, Mary II and the Bill of Rights

Parliament offered the throne jointly to William and Mary in February 1689. Before they were crowned, they had to accept the Bill of Rights (December 1689). This document was pivotal: it confirmed that the monarch could not suspend laws, levy taxes or maintain a peacetime army without parliamentary consent. Free elections to Parliament were guaranteed, as was free speech within Parliament. The Bill of Rights did not create a democracy — it protected the rights of property-owning Protestant men — but it fundamentally shifted power away from the Crown towards Parliament.

The Bill of Rights banned several specific royal actions: suspending laws without parliamentary consent, establishing church courts without consent, keeping a standing army in peacetime without consent, and imposing taxes without Parliament. It also guaranteed the right to petition the monarch, prohibited excessive bail and cruel punishments, and protected the right of Protestants to bear arms for self-defence. These clauses directly responded to James II’s specific actions.

The Act of Settlement 1701 and the Hanoverian Succession

When it became clear that William III and Anne (Mary’s sister, who succeeded in 1702) would leave no Protestant heirs, Parliament passed the Act of Settlement in 1701. This barred Catholics and anyone married to a Catholic from the throne. The Crown was to pass to Sophia of Hanover, granddaughter of James I, and her Protestant heirs. When Anne died in 1714, the succession passed peacefully to George I, the first Hanoverian king, despite over 50 closer blood relatives who were Catholic and therefore excluded. This was a deliberate constitutional choice: religion, not bloodline, now determined who could rule England.

Key Fact

Key constitutional landmarks: Bill of Rights (1689) — limits on Crown; Toleration Act (1689) — Protestant Dissenters allowed to worship; Act of Settlement (1701) — Protestant-only succession; Act of Union with Scotland (1707); George I crowned (1714).

The Glorious Revolution did not affect only England. In Ireland, it triggered a war (the Williamite War 1689–1691) that ended in Williamite victory at the Boyne and Aughrim, followed by the Penal Laws against Catholics. In Scotland, a separate Jacobite uprising at Killiecrankie (1689) was defeated. The succession settlement of 1701 was one of the pressures that pushed Scotland towards the Act of Union 1707. The Hanoverian succession in 1714 was not universally accepted — the Jacobite rising of 1715 (“the Fifteen”) attempted to restore the Stuart line.

Significance of the Revolution

The constitutional settlement of 1688–1701 had lasting consequences for England’s global power. By tying the Crown to Parliament and to Protestant merchant interests, it created stable conditions for the financial revolution of the 1690s — including the founding of the Bank of England (1694) and the growth of the national debt, which funded the wars of William III against Louis XIV of France. The Bill of Rights and Act of Settlement together made England a constitutional monarchy — not an absolute one like France — and this distinction shaped its economic and imperial trajectory throughout the eighteenth century.
exam_tip_html: For a “Describe Two Features” question on the Glorious Revolution, give two distinct, factually specific points — for example, the landing at Brixham (November 1688) and the Bill of Rights (December 1689). Avoid vague phrases like “it changed things.” For a “Significance” question, you must show both short-term and long-term impact and consider how significant the change actually was — examiners reward judgements that weigh the consequences rather than simply listing them.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • William of Orange landed at Brixham in November 1688; James II fled to France; William and Mary were jointly crowned in February 1689 on condition of accepting the Bill of Rights.
  • The Bill of Rights (1689) limited royal power over law, taxation and the army; the Act of Settlement (1701) permanently excluded Catholics from the throne and secured a Protestant Hanoverian succession.
  • The term “Glorious Revolution” reflects a Whig perspective — for Irish Catholics and Jacobites the same events were a conquest and a dispossession; the constitutional settlement created conditions for England’s financial and imperial expansion.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Bill of Rights (1689).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise identification with accurate supporting detail (e.g. it prohibited the monarch from suspending laws without Parliament's consent). Secure: Correct feature with some supporting information. Developing: Vague reference to limiting royal power without specific detail. Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Act of Settlement (1701).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise, distinct features each with accurate supporting detail. Secure: Two features identified, at least one with supporting detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two features stated without detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Glorious Revolution of 1688 was significant for England's constitutional development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed, sustained explanation linking at least two causes or consequences with precise evidence (e.g. Bill of Rights limitations, Act of Settlement, financial revolution context). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one consequence explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive rather than analytical. Emerging: Simple or vague points; limited or missing evidence.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Glorious Revolution (1688) for reshaping the relationship between Crown and Parliament in England? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, multi-perspective argument evaluating short- and long-term significance, integrating precise evidence and considering counter-arguments (e.g. limitations of the Bill of Rights, Jacobite opposition). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence showing both significance and limitation. Developing: Some argument with basic evidence; may focus on only one dimension. Emerging: Simple points with limited or no evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why some contemporaries did not view the events of 1688 as a 'Glorious Revolution'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation with precise evidence showing a specific perspective (e.g. Irish Catholic, Jacobite) and why events were experienced as loss or conquest. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason given with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the constitutional settlement of 1689–1701.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise, distinct features (e.g. Bill of Rights, Act of Settlement) each with accurate supporting detail. Secure: Two features identified, at least one with supporting detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two features without detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

What did the Act of Settlement (1701) primarily establish?
options: A Catholic succession to the throne
The right of Parliament to tax the Crown
A standing army for the monarch

knowledge_checks.q: The Bill of Rights was passed in December _____.
The first Hanoverian king, _____, succeeded to the throne in 1714.
Match each constitutional document to its key provision:
right: Protestant Dissenters allowed to worship openly
Parliament must consent to taxation and standing armies

flashcard_questions.q: When did William of Orange land at Brixham?
What was James II accused of doing that triggered the invitation to William?
flashcard_questions.a: Promoting Catholics, suspending anti-Catholic laws, and fathering a Catholic heir

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Bill of Rights passed?
Name three things the Bill of Rights prohibited the monarch from doing.
flashcard_questions.a: Suspending laws, levying taxes, or keeping a standing army — all without parliamentary consent

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Act of Settlement (1701) establish?
flashcard_questions.a: A Protestant-only succession; Catholics barred from the throne

flashcard_questions.q: Who was the first Hanoverian king and when did he accede?
Why is the term 'Glorious Revolution' contested?
flashcard_questions.a: It reflects a Whig/Protestant view; Irish Catholics and Jacobites experienced it as conquest
It allowed Protestant Dissenters to worship openly, though Catholics were excluded

flashcard_questions.q: What was John Churchill's significance in 1688?
flashcard_questions.a: He defected from James II to William, contributing to the king's collapse of support

flashcard_questions.q: How did the Glorious Revolution enable the financial revolution?
flashcard_questions.a: Stable parliamentary monarchy underpinned the Bank of England (1694) and national debt funding for war

glossary_terms.definition: King of England, Scotland and Ireland 1685–1688, a Catholic monarch whose policies alarmed Protestant landowners and Parliament.
Dutch Protestant prince and Stadholder of the Dutch Republic who was invited to invade England in 1688.
The 1689 law that set out the constitutional limits on royal power, including rights of Parliament to free elections, free speech and regular sessions.
The 1701 law that settled the Crown on the Protestant Hanoverian line, excluding Catholics from the succession.
